chunks: Abu Ali Al-Ash'ari, from Muhammad ibn Abd al-Jabbar, from Safwan ibn Yahya, from Ibn Miskan, from Abu Baseer, from one of the Imams (peace be upon him), who said:

I asked him about the Statement of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: 'And who is more unjust than he who forges a lie against Allah or says: It has been revealed to me,' while nothing has been revealed to him.'

He said: It was revealed regarding Ibn Abi Sarh, whom Uthman appointed as governor over Egypt. He was among those with the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) on the Day of the Conquest of Mecca, whose blood was spared. He used to write for the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family).

So when Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed: 'Surely Allah is Mighty, Wise,' he would write: 'Surely Allah is Knowing, Wise.' So the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) would say to him: Leave it, for surely Allah is Knowing, Wise.
And Ibn Abi Sarh used to say to the hypocrites: 'I say from myself similar to what he brings, so he does not alter it for me.'
So Allah, Blessed and Exalted, revealed regarding him what He revealed.

key_terms.ابْنُ أَبِي سَرْحٍ: Ibn Abi Sarh, a companion and scribe of the Prophet
key_terms.هَدَرَ دَمَهُ: His blood was spared (not killed) during the Conquest of Mecca
key_terms.يَوْمَ فَتْحِ مَكَّةَ: The Day of the Conquest of Mecca

ai.seo_question: Who is Ibn Abi Sarh and what is his connection to the verse 'And who is more unjust than he who forges a lie against Allah?'
ai.summary: This hadith identifies Ibn Abi Sarh as the specific individual for whom the verse 'Who is more unjust than one who invents a lie about Allah...' was revealed, highlighting his role as the Prophet's scribe who substituted 'Allah is Knowing' for 'Allah is Mighty' to facilitate memorization. In Shia scholarship, this incident is often cited to illustrate the precision of the Prophet's dictation and the divine protection of the Quranic text from even minor alterations by his trusted scribes. The narrative underscores the transition from his initial acceptance to his eventual apostasy, marking him as a key figure in the early history of the Quran's compilation.
